This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.

This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.

—Grace Huckins

Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths

Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.

Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.

Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.

—Sara Kiley Watson

This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue.

articles.title: K9 Vajra-T vs K9A2: Did India Make the Right Choice?
articles.text:
Should the Indian Army proceed with procuring further K9 Vajra-T systems, or wait to procure the upgraded K9A2 variant from South Korea? Overall it makes sense to proceed with procuring the current variant of the K9 Vajra-T. This will help meet immediate artillery requirements, adding to an existing fleet provides benefits such as ease of training, maintenance and logistics. However, obtaining an agreement to future upgrade to the K9A2 variant will provide strategic benefits.
On 26 th October 2026, the DAC reportedly gave AoN for 335 more tracked self-propelled guns, which have been widely reported in the media as being the K9 Vajra-T. The MoD did not state how many they were procuring or the value. AoN does not mean they have signed the procurement contract.
This would add to the 100 K9 Vajra-T guns delivered under the original contract in 2017. It would also add to the 100 signed in December 2024. If they do sign the contract for 335 more guns, India would have 535 in total.
Having one major tracked self-propelled artillery family means there will be benefits in training, maintenance, spares and ammunition qualification. It also helps the army and domestic industry as they can take advantage of the existing production lines in India.
This latest procurement has a high indigenous content of over 70%, which can benefit domestic production. However, how much we are truly self-sufficient will depend on what key components are manufactured domestically. What Does the K9A2 Bring?
The K9A2 is an upgraded version of the existing K9 family. The major changes have been made to automate the system and reduce the number of crew members.
It will include an automatic loader for the projectile and charge, giving a rate of fire of around 9-10 rounds per minute. This is an improvement from around 6-8 rounds per minute of previous variants. The K9A2 will also include an electric turret drive and several other enhancements to reduce the number of crew members down to 3.
This could improve long term efficiency, reduce manpower requirements and help increase the speed of fire missions from the artillery units. The major differences between the K9A2 and the rest of the family are not the increased barrel length, but increased automation of the turret. Waiting to procure a large amount of these systems may mean the artillery formations will have to wait to get the upgraded version.
The K9 Vajra-T is already in service within India and has been modified for the Indian environment. This means we can continue to procure them to keep consistency. We will not be introducing a new variant before understanding the maturity, production lines and lifecycle costs.
India have other requirements to consider. Being able to deploy at high altitudes, operate in cold environments and having mobility, electronic protection and protection from drones and loitering munitions is becoming more important. The major risk is not procuring the K9 Vajra-T now, but not having a realistic upgrade path for hundreds more.
We should try and obtain a realistic upgrade path to include automation, turret drives and fewer crew members. Any proposal should include the costs of upgrading the existing vehicles, importing components and the impact on the guns. Overall it makes sense to continue with the K9 Vajra-T as it meets our immediate requirement and keeps consistency. The K9A2 provides a realistic upgrade path to increase automation and reduce workload.
